title: Relative Abhyankar inequality for a valued field extension
statement: Let $F\subseteq K$ be fields [def-weil-field] such that $K$ is finitely generated as a field over $F$, and let $A$ be a valuation ring of $K$, i.e. a subring $A\subseteq K$ such that for every $a\in K^\times$ at least one of $a,a^{-1}$ lies in $A$ (so $A$ is local with fraction field $K$; write $\mathfrak m_A$ for its maximal ideal and $A^\times$ for its unit group). Put $A_F=A\cap F$; it is a valuation ring of $F$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_{A_F}=\mathfrak m_A\cap F$ and unit group $A_F^\times=A^\times\cap F^\times$. Let $\Gamma_K=K^\times/A^\times$ and $\Gamma_F=F^\times/A_F^\times$; the inclusion $F^\times\subseteq K^\times$ induces an injective homomorphism $\Gamma_F\hookrightarrow\Gamma_K$. Let $\kappa_K=A/\mathfrak m_A$ and $\kappa_F=A_F/\mathfrak m_{A_F}$, with the induced field embedding $\kappa_F\hookrightarrow\kappa_K$. For an abelian group $G$ put $\operatorname{rrk}(G)=\dim_{\mathbf Q}(G\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q)$. Then $\operatorname{rrk}(\Gamma_K/\Gamma_F)+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa_F}\kappa_K\le\operatorname{trdeg}_F K$, where $\Gamma_K/\Gamma_F$ is the quotient abelian group. Here transcendence degree and algebraic independence have the meaning of [def-kun-transcendence-degree].

source.place: §2.1, Lemma 2.1.2 (Abhyankar inequality) and Corollary 2.1.3(i) for the height consequence; the local document copy is unavailable.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finitely-generated-field-finite-transcendence-basis] to $K/F$. Its finite transcendence basis and [def-kun-transcendence-degree] give $d=\operatorname{trdeg}_F K<\infty$. Put $H=\Gamma_K/\Gamma_F$, $V=H\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$, and for $z\in K^\times$ write $q(z)\in V$ for the image of its class. We use additive notation in $H$ and $V$, so $q(zw)=q(z)+q(w)$ and $q(c)=0$ for $c\in F^\times$.

Fix arbitrary integers $r,s\geq0$, elements $x_1,\ldots,x_r\in K^\times$ for which $q(x_1),\ldots,q(x_r)$ are $\mathbf Q$-linearly independent, and elements $y_1,\ldots,y_s\in A$ whose residues $\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar y_s$ are algebraically independent over $\kappa_F$ [def-kun-transcendence-degree]. Linear independence means that a relation $\sum_i a_iq(x_i)=0$ with $a_i\in\mathbf Q$ has all $a_i=0$. The empty families are permitted. Steps 3--6 show directly that no nonzero polynomial over $F$ vanishes on the combined indexed family $(x_1,\ldots,x_r,y_1,\ldots,y_s)$.

proof.text: For each nonzero polynomial $P\in F[Y_1,\ldots,Y_s]$, choose a nonzero coefficient $c$ such that every coefficient divided by $c$ belongs to $A_F$. Such a choice exists by finite selection: for two nonzero coefficients $a,b$, either $a/b\in A_F$ or $b/a\in A_F$; keep the divisor, and process the remaining coefficients. Then $P/c$ has coefficients in $A_F$, and one coefficient is $1$. Its reduction is therefore a nonzero polynomial over $\kappa_F$. Algebraic independence of the residues gives $(P/c)(y)\bmod\mathfrak m_A\ne0$. Thus $P(y)/c$ belongs to $A\setminus\mathfrak m_A=A^\times$. In particular $P(y)\ne0$ and $P(y)=cu_P$ for some $u_P\in A^\times$. The identity of residue evaluation follows term by term because reduction preserves sums and products.

source.place: Tag 0ASH, lemma-inequality-general, proof: minimum-term normalization. Agent-written polynomial analogue, not an application of the finite-extension statement. The original Temkin Lemma 2.1.2 is unavailable locally.

proof.text: Let $Q\in F[X_1,\ldots,X_r,Y_1,\ldots,Y_s]$ be nonzero. Group its terms by their $X$-exponents to write $Q=\sum_{\alpha\in I}X^\alpha P_\alpha(Y)$, with $I$ a finite nonempty set of distinct tuples in $\mathbf N^r$ and every $P_\alpha\ne0$. By Step 3, $P_\alpha(y)=c_\alpha u_\alpha$ with $c_\alpha\in F^\times$ and $u_\alpha\in A^\times$. Hence $T_\alpha=x^\alpha P_\alpha(y)$ is nonzero. For distinct $\alpha,\beta$, its quotient $T_\alpha/T_\beta$ cannot be a unit of $A$: otherwise taking its image under $q$ gives $0=\sum_i(\alpha_i-\beta_i)q(x_i)$, since $q(c_\alpha/c_\beta)=0$ and units map to zero. Linear independence forces $\alpha_i=\beta_i$ for every $i$, a contradiction.

To do this, start with one term and process the others: keep the current choice when the new term divided by it lies in $A$; otherwise the inverse quotient lies in $A$, so replace the choice by the new term. proof.text: By Steps 3--5 and [def-kun-transcendence-degree], the combined indexed family is algebraically independent over $F$. Its entries are distinct: equality of two entries would give the nonzero relation $Z_i-Z_j$ in the corresponding two distinct variables. Its underlying set thus has $r+s$ elements, and the definition of transcendence degree gives $r+s\le d$. This conclusion holds for every pair of finite families chosen in Step 2, including $r=0$ or $s=0$.

proof.text: The elements $q(z)$, $z\in K^\times$, span $V$: a tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors $h\otimes a=a(h\otimes1)$, and every $h\in H$ is represented by a class of some $z\in K^\times$. Starting from the empty family, if the selected $q(z)$ do not span, some $q(z)$ is outside their span and can be added while preserving independence (in a relation with its coefficient nonzero, solve for that element to contradict its choice). Step 6 with $s=0$ forbids $d+1$ such elements, so this procedure stops after $a\le d$ choices with a basis of $V$. Its cardinality is $a=\dim_{\mathbf Q}V=\operatorname{rrk}(H)$. This establishes finiteness before using ordinary integer dimension; no finite generation or torsion-freeness of $H$ has been assumed.

source.place: Tag 0ASH, lemma-inequality-general, proof: minimum-term normalization. Agent-written polynomial analogue, not an application of the finite-extension statement. The original Temkin Lemma 2.1.2 is unavailable locally.

proof.text: By Step 6 with $r=0$, every finite algebraically independent subset of $\kappa_K$ over $\kappa_F$ has size at most $d$. An infinite such subset would contain $d+1$ distinct elements, so none exists. The possible sizes therefore form a nonempty subset of $\{0,\ldots,d\}$, containing $0$, with maximum $b$. By [def-kun-transcendence-degree] this maximum is $b=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa_F}\kappa_K$. Choose a family attaining $b$ and lift each entry along the surjection $A\to\kappa_K$. Combine it with the $a$ elements chosen in Step 7. Step 6 now gives $a+b\le d$, which is exactly the asserted relative Abhyankar inequality.
